extracted.intended_audience: academic researchers, journal editors, and stakeholders in scholarly publishing
extracted.subtask_description: Normative guidance and expectations for how journals and researchers should act regarding journal prestige, impact factors, and related research-assessment practices. Covers actions journals can take and considerations researchers should make when boycotting or criticizing top-tier journals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not promote the impact factor metric
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals should avoid promoting the impact factor metric when presenting themselves to authors or readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes eLife's 'declared policy of not promoting the impact factor metric' as a positive example and criticizes journals for trumpeting single-figure averages. Anti-pattern: using impact factor as a marketing pitch to attract submissions or readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reveal detailed citation data behind impact factor averages
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals should publish the citation-detail behind the single-figure averages (impact factors) to demystify the metric.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Nature Materials 'revealed the detail of the citation data behind the single-figure averages' — this practice should become standard as it would help demystify the allure of this quality proxy. Guidance: provide breakdowns rather than only headline impact-factor numbers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sign or meaningfully engage with DORA (San Francisco Declaration on Research Assessment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals should sign up to or actively engage with DORA to help neutralise the poisonous effect of impact factors on science and careers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author asks why Nature has not signed DORA and suggests journals either sign or explain specific objections and 'explore ways around them.' Scoring guidance: full support = sign DORA; partial = publicly explain objections and propose actionable compromises; none = no engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journals must accept responsibility as part of the research community
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals should not simply lay the problem of impact-factor obsession at the feet of researchers; they are part of the community and must act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The piece argues 'it is not sufficient to lay the problem at the feet of the research community when journals are part of that community.' Expectation: journals take proactive policy changes rather than only editorial commentaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid marketing that emphasizes impact factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Editorial/marketing efforts should refrain from advertising impact factors when 'pitching for authors or readers.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author criticises shrugging off impact-factor promotion as 'the work of the marketing department.' Recommended practice: remove impact-factor boasting from solicitation materials and marketing copy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be transparent about objections to reform proposals and work to resolve them
rubrics_metrics.description: If a journal declines to endorse reform initiatives (e.g., DORA), it should explain specific objections and explore ways around them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Philip Campbell's comment that 'the draft statement contained many specific elements, some of which were too sweeping' is cited — the author suggests 'It would be helpful to know more about Nature’s objections, to explore ways around them.' Transparency + constructive engagement is expected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Those who take public stands must mitigate risks to junior researchers
rubrics_metrics.description: Researchers who boycott or publicly refuse to publish in top-tier journals should consider and mitigate the potential career risks to junior lab members.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author asks for clarity on 'how he talked through the move with his group and how he aims to mitigate the risks to the junior members’ careers?' Guidance: explain consultation with group, concrete mitigation plans (e.g., alternative publication strategies, letters of support), and be mindful of downstream career impacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclose and consider conflicts of interest and optics
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors and senior researchers should acknowledge and disclose conflicts of interest and be mindful of perceived hypocrisy when criticizing institutions that helped their careers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article observes Schekman was 'branded as hypocritical' because he 'owes much of his success to the journals he has denounced' and has a 'clear conflict of interest as editor-in-chief at eLife.' Recommended practice: transparent disclosure of past affiliations and reflection on optics when leading reform efforts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Take concrete actions beyond editorials and reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals should move beyond editorial comment and reporting about problems with impact factors and adopt concrete policies and practices to change culture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author states 'it is not sufficient to lay the problem at the feet of the research community' and that Nature has 'done a good job drawing attention' but 'can do more.' Examples of concrete actions include policy changes, data transparency, and signing reform declarations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support and invest time in alternative publishing models that avoid harmful metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Senior scientists and journals should commit time and effort to alternative journals and practices that do not promote impact-factor-driven assessment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example cited: Schekman 'committing time to eLife' which aspires to be top-tier but has policies against promoting impact factors. Guidance: leadership and resource commitment to alternatives is a meaningful step toward culture change.
